text: Risk is not determined by the action alone. Which additional factors does the module say determine an action's risk? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Where the change is applied
options.why: Yes. Editing a README and editing .github/workflows/ are the same verb with very different consequences.

options.text: How easily the change can be reversed
options.why: Yes. Reversibility is the pivot: full automation is appropriate only when failures are reversible.

options.text: How quickly it affects users or systems
options.why: Yes. Blast speed determines how much time a control has to catch a problem before it reaches production.

options.text: How many lines of code the change contains
options.why: No. Diff size is a poor proxy - workflow and infrastructure paths are explicitly called out as "small diff, big consequence" areas.

takeaway: Classify risk by location, reversibility, and speed of impact - never by diff size.

text: Which autonomy level describes an agent that can create branches and pull requests but cannot merge or deploy?

options.text: Read-only autonomy
options.why: Read-only means the agent can inspect, summarize, classify, and recommend, but cannot modify anything - including creating branches.

options.text: Propose-only autonomy
options.why: Propose-only is exactly this level: the agent can create branches and pull requests but cannot merge or deploy. It is the level that implements "agents propose; humans and policy accept".

options.text: Execute with guardrails
options.why: That level allows running pre-approved workflows such as tests, builds, and staging deploys within defined limits.

options.text: Human-authorized execution
options.why: That level allows high-impact actions - production deploys, workflow changes, secret access - but only after a human approves.

takeaway: Four levels: read-only, propose-only, execute with guardrails, and human-authorized execution. Autonomy is usually a combination of controls, not one setting.

text: A team wants to grow agent autonomy safely over several quarters. Which progression matches the module's guidance?

options.text: Start with production deploy access and remove permissions if incidents occur.
options.why: This starts at maximum blast radius and learns from damage. Progressive autonomy starts strict and relaxes on evidence.

options.text: Open pull requests only, then merge low-risk PRs after checks, then deploy to staging automatically, then deploy to production only through environment approval.
options.why: This is the documented safe progression. Teams begin with strict controls and relax them gradually as agent behavior proves reliable, so autonomy scales on evidence rather than optimism.

options.text: Grant full autonomy in a sandbox repository, then copy the same settings to production repositories.
options.why: Sandbox behavior does not transfer: the risk profile of the repository, not the agent's sandbox record, determines appropriate controls.

options.text: Alternate weekly between full and read-only autonomy to gather comparative data.
options.why: Unpredictable capability makes both the agent and the review process unreliable, and it gathers noise rather than evidence.

takeaway: Progressive autonomy: PRs only, then low-risk merges after checks, then automatic staging deploys, then production only via environment approval.

text: An agent emits a plan with a risk rating. What is the recommended way to act on that rating?

options.text: Include a narrative risk paragraph in the PR description for reviewers to interpret.
options.why: The guidance is explicit: do not rely on narrative explanations of risk. Interpretation varies between reviewers and cannot be enforced.

options.text: Emit a machine-readable signal, such as a risk field in plan.json, and route execution on it - low risk applies automatically, anything else goes to a job in an approval-gated environment.
options.why: Reading the risk value into a job output and using it in an if: condition to choose between an auto-apply job and an approval-gated one enforces the decision consistently, rather than leaving it to interpretation.

options.text: Have the agent decide for itself whether approval is needed.
options.why: The agent proposing the rating and enforcing it are different responsibilities. Enforcement belongs to the workflow.

options.text: Apply the strictest gate to every plan regardless of the rating.
options.why: That discards the rating entirely and reintroduces approval fatigue on low-risk work.

takeaway: Emit risk as a machine-readable signal and enforce routing on it. Narrative risk is not a control.

text: Which decision points should human oversight be placed at, according to the module? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Merge
options.why: Yes. Merge is where a proposal becomes part of the codebase.

options.text: Deployment
options.why: Yes. Deployment is where a change reaches users and systems.

options.text: Access to sensitive resources such as production secrets
options.why: Yes. Secret access is a named high-impact decision point.

options.text: Every analysis and formatting step the agent performs
options.why: No. The guidance is to put humans at decision points, not at every step - analysis, formatting, and routine checks should flow automatically.

takeaway: Humans at merge, deploy, and secret access. Analysis, formatting, and routine checks stay automated.

text: A terminal agent should search and read freely, but any edit or command execution must be approved at the time of use. How do you express that?

options.text: Grant all tools and instruct the agent to ask before editing.
options.why: Asking is voluntary. Tool-based approval boundaries are a control; instructions are not.

options.text: Allow the low-risk tools explicitly - for example --allow-tool 'read,search' - leaving edit and execute available but approval-gated at the point of use.
options.why: This is the tool-based approval boundary pattern: it removes friction for low-risk tools while ensuring high-risk tools remain available but require explicit approval when they are actually invoked.

options.text: Remove the edit and execute tools entirely.
options.why: That removes the capability rather than gating it, so the agent can never do the work even when a human would approve.

options.text: Require a human to approve the whole session before it starts.
options.why: A blanket session approval cannot distinguish the read the human intended from the destructive edit they did not.

takeaway: Auto-allow low-risk tools; leave high-risk tools available but approval-gated at the moment of use.

text: Your organization wants sudo, rm -rf /, and curl-piped-to-bash blocked before a local agent can execute them. What implements this?

options.text: A banner printed at session start warning against dangerous commands.
options.why: The guidance is blunt: logging and banners are helpful, but they do not prevent execution.

options.text: A Copilot CLI preToolUse hook with deny rules matching those patterns for shell tools.
options.why: A preToolUse hook with permissionDecision: deny rules turns policy into a technical control by blocking the command before execution, reducing the risk of unintended or destructive actions.

options.text: A CODEOWNERS entry for the scripts directory.
options.why: CODEOWNERS routes review of file changes. It cannot intercept a command at runtime.

options.text: A required status check that scans commits for those strings.
options.why: A check runs after a commit exists. The hook prevents the command from running at all.

takeaway: Use enforceable hooks for blocking. If the platform cannot enforce it, it will eventually be bypassed.

text: A team needs a rule that branch protection settings cannot express: agent-authored pull requests must never be approved solely by another bot. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Accept the limitation - if settings cannot express it, it cannot be enforced.
options.why: Guardrail workflows exist precisely to enforce rules that are not expressible via settings alone.

options.text: Add a guardrail workflow that inspects reviews via the API and fails the check unless at least one approval comes from a human user.
options.why: This is the defense-in-depth pattern: a workflow that lists PR reviews and calls core.setFailed unless an approval exists from a user account that is not the agent identity. You still keep branch protections and CODEOWNERS - the guardrail workflow adds what settings cannot express.

options.text: Remove the agent's ability to open pull requests.
options.why: That eliminates the workflow rather than governing it.

options.text: Document the rule in CONTRIBUTING.md and rely on reviewer discipline.
options.why: "Controls in docs only" is a named anti-pattern.

takeaway: Layer enforcement: rulesets and CODEOWNERS for what settings can express, guardrail workflows for what they cannot.

text: The layered enforcement model spans three stages. Which listing is correct?

options.text: Pre-action constraints (permissions), in-action validation (checks), post-action traceability (logs and artifacts).
options.why: These are the three layers. The accompanying rule is decisive: if a control is not enforced by the platform, treat it as optional.

options.text: Planning review, implementation review, deployment review.
options.why: These are review moments, not the enforcement layers the module defines.

options.text: Repository rules, organization rules, enterprise rules.
options.why: That is a scope hierarchy, not the temporal enforcement model.

options.text: Authentication, authorization, auditing.
options.why: A reasonable general security triad, but not the model taught here.

takeaway: Constrain before (permissions), validate during (checks), trace after (logs and artifacts) - and treat unenforced controls as optional.

text: Beyond the permissions block, which additional controls support least-privilege agent execution? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Restrict secrets access using environments
options.why: Yes. Environment-scoped secrets mean a job that does not target the environment cannot read them.

options.text: Isolate workflows so high-risk jobs do not share permissions with low-risk jobs
options.why: Yes. Separation stops a low-risk job inheriting capability it never needs.

options.text: Minimize third-party actions and pin versions where possible
options.why: Yes. Every third-party action is executing code inside your permission context; fewer and pinned reduces that exposure.

options.text: Store a broadly scoped personal access token as a repository secret for convenience
options.why: No. A broad PAT is the excess-permissions anti-pattern - a small mistake becomes a major incident.

takeaway: Least privilege is layered: minimal permissions, environment-scoped secrets, workflow isolation, and minimal pinned third-party actions.

text: For a protected branch such as main, which rules should a ruleset enforce for agent-driven work? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Require a pull request to merge and require checks to pass
options.why: Yes. These make the PR the mandatory path and evaluation an enforceable gate.

options.text: Require approving reviews per risk, including CODEOWNERS review for sensitive paths
options.why: Yes - and note the caveat: unless "require CODEOWNERS review" is enabled, CODEOWNERS is advisory only.

options.text: Restrict direct pushes and block force pushes and branch deletion
options.why: Yes. These close the bypass paths that would otherwise let policy be skipped.

options.text: Require every pull request to be squash-merged
options.why: No. Merge strategy is a history-shape preference, not a governance control for agent work.

takeaway: Protected-branch rules: PR required, checks required, reviews per risk with CODEOWNERS on sensitive paths, no direct or force pushes, no branch deletion.

text: Six months after setup, required checks have been renamed, CODEOWNERS lists people who left, and several workflow tokens now hold write permissions. What is this, and what is the remedy?

options.text: A configuration bug; restore the repository from a backup.
options.why: Each individual change was probably deliberate and reasonable at the time. The failure is cumulative, not a single fault.

options.text: Governance drift; treat governance as an ongoing operational responsibility with a periodic review cadence - weekly failed runs and policy violations, monthly permissions and secret scopes, quarterly rulesets, CODEOWNERS, environment reviewers, and retention.
options.why: Controls degrade as checks are renamed or removed, review requirements are relaxed, CODEOWNERS goes stale, permissions expand, and secrets move into broader scopes. The prescribed answer is a continuous governance loop on that cadence.

options.text: Normal evolution; no action is needed as long as no incident has occurred.
options.why: Waiting for an incident is how small gaps accumulate into a large one.

options.text: Excess permissions only; revoke all write tokens.
options.why: That addresses one symptom and leaves the stale checks and ownership untouched.

takeaway: Governance drifts. Run the loop: weekly failures and violations, monthly permissions and secrets, quarterly rulesets, ownership, reviewers, and retention.

text: Match the governance anti-pattern to its mitigation: approvals have become "click to unblock" and nobody actually reviews.

options.text: Unbounded autonomy; add environments with required reviewers.
options.why: That anti-pattern is having no approval at all for production deploys. Here approvals exist - they are just hollow.

options.text: Rubber-stamping; fix it with better evidence, CODEOWNERS routing, and smaller pull requests.
options.why: Rubber-stamping is the named anti-pattern where approvals become a formality. The mitigation is making review genuinely easy: attach evidence so review is fast, route to people with context, and keep PRs small enough to actually read.

options.text: Missing audit trail; fix it with artifact uploads.
options.why: That is about being unable to prove what happened, not about approvals losing meaning.

options.text: Bypass paths exist; fix it with branch protections.
options.why: Bypass paths are direct pushes to main or disabled checks - policy being skipped rather than performed emptily.

takeaway: Rubber-stamping is fixed by making review worth doing: good evidence, targeted routing, and small scope.

text: A change is ready to merge but no artifacts, plan, or execution report were produced. What does the governance module say to do?

options.text: Merge it - the required checks passed, which is the enforceable signal.
options.why: Passing checks is necessary, not sufficient. The module treats missing evidence as a failure in its own right.

options.text: Treat missing evidence as a failure: if a change cannot be audited, it should not be merged.
options.why: The rule is stated directly - missing evidence equals failure. Without durable evidence you cannot debug reliably, investigate incidents, prove compliance, or trust autonomous changes over time.

options.text: Merge it and backfill evidence afterwards from the run logs.
options.why: Logs expire under retention and cannot reconstruct a plan that was never produced.

options.text: Merge it but add a label indicating evidence was missing.
options.why: A label records the gap without closing it, and the unauditable change still lands.

takeaway: Missing evidence = failure. Every meaningful action must leave a trace a reviewer can inspect.

text: Under the observability model, what must every meaningful agent action produce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Pull request and commit history
options.why: Yes. What changed, and in what sequence.

options.text: Workflow results including job logs, timing, and the acting identity
options.why: Yes. What ran, how long it took, and who or what ran it.

options.text: Uploaded artifacts such as a plan, test results, or an execution report - and for production, the environment approval record
options.why: Yes. Machine-readable evidence such as plan.json and execution-report, plus approval and merge events, is what makes the action auditable.

options.text: A screenshot of the agent's chat session attached to the pull request
options.why: No. Chat screenshots are neither machine-readable nor authoritative. Evidence-first workflows output structured artifacts.

takeaway: Produce PR and commits, workflow results with actor and timing, structured artifacts, and approval and merge events - including the environment approval record for production.
